Reason.headline: Your brain runs on tiny batteries.
Reason.subhead: Billions of them. And they’re the reason you feel sharp — or you don’t.
Reason.bodyP1: Your brain is the hungriest organ you own. It never stops, and it never coasts.
Reason.bodyP2: All that energy is made by billions of microscopic batteries inside your cells — the mitochondria. When they’re full and firing, you feel it. Quick. Clear. On.
Reason.bodyP3: But like every battery, they fade with time. Scientists call it mitochondrial decay. As the batteries weaken, the brain gets less energy — and you feel that too: the name that slips, the 3 p.m. fog.
Reason.turn: But batteries can be looked after.
Reason.surface: Coffee rents you sharpness for an afternoon. This is about making more of the energy itself.
Reason.differentiation: Not at the surface. At the source.
Reason.pivot: Three papers in one issue of PNAS drew the roadmap — cited 22,000+ times since.
Reason.calloutLabel: of your body / of its energy
Reason.visualAlt: A charged mitochondrion, clearly structured, beside dimmer fading ones

Scientist.headline: Thirty years. One question.
Scientist.subhead: Neuroscientist Dr. Jiankang Liu has spent a career on how a brain keeps its energy.
Scientist.journalFull: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
Scientist.plateNote: Three papers from that issue — the research behind NuriCell.
Scientist.bodyP1: PNAS — the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences — is one of the most cited journals in the world. Most researchers never place a single paper there. In February 2002, one issue carried three of his.
Scientist.bodyP2: What the papers showed, in plain words: fed two natural compounds — acetyl-L-carnitine and alpha-lipoic acid — old rats worked memory tests the way young ones did, and their failing mitochondria recovered.
Scientist.bodyP3: It’s a life’s work focused on one idea: how the brain makes its energy, and how to help it keep making it. The question he asked about aging brains is the one you’re asking about yours.
Scientist.bodyP4: When our founder, Mo Chen, set out to build BiGH, he didn’t start with a logo or a launch plan. He started with a scientist he’s known for years — and the belief that this research deserved to reach the people who need it.
Scientist.pivot: His research became a formula. We call it NuriCell.
Scientist.photoAlt: The table of contents of PNAS volume 99, number 4, February 19, 2002

beat3.headline: Two nutrients. Greater together.
beat3.body: Acetyl-L-carnitine feeds the brain’s batteries; alpha-lipoic acid defends them. Alone, each helps. Together, in his studies, old rats recovered memory — and their mitochondria recovered with them.
beat3.unionNote: The overlap is the discovery — together they restored mitochondrial function, and memory, in aging animals.
